```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
library(pixarfilms)
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)

```
## 1. Introduction
In this project, we analyze the Pixar Film Ratings dataset to understand the relationship 
between critical acclaim and commercial success. Our objective is to explore how 
audience perceptions and critic scores have evolved over the years and their 
impact on the studio's financial performance.

The report covers the full workflow: data cleaning and preparation, exploratory data analysis (EDA), statistical modeling (linear and logistic regression), and a final reflection.


## 2. Data Cleaning and Preparation

### 2.1. Loading and Merging the Datasets

In this step, we load the three main tables from the `pixarfilms` package: `pixar_films`, `pixar_ratings`, and `pixar_box_office`. 
To conduct a comprehensive analysis, we merge these datasets into a single "Master Dataset" using the common `film` column as our primary key.

Before merging, we inspect each dataset individually. 
`pixar_films` contains 27 films with basic information: film number, name, release date, runtime, and rating. 
`public_response` contains 24 rows with critic scores from Rotten Tomatoes, Metacritic, CinemaScore, and Critics' Choice (the last row, *Luca*, has no scores yet). 
`box_office` also contains 24 rows with budget and revenue data (again, the *Luca* row is empty). 

We noticed that `pixar_films` lists 27 films while scores and box office figures are only available for the first 23 — 
the 4 most recent entries (*Luca*, *Turning Red*, *Lightyear* and an untitled 2023 film whose `film` value is `NA`) have no critic scores or financial data in this version of the package. 
These films were released, but the package simply does not contain their figures (several of them premiered directly on Disney+ and therefore have no box office). 

We also notice that `number` is stored as text (`chr`) in `pixar_films` and will need to be fixed after merging. 
We use `film` as the join key since it appears in all three tables.

```{r}
# Loading original datasets from the package
pixar_films <- pixarfilms::pixar_films
pixar_ratings <- pixarfilms::public_response
pixar_box_office <- pixarfilms::box_office

# Inspecting each dataset before merging
str(pixar_films)
str(pixar_ratings)
str(pixar_box_office)

```
After merging, the `master dataset` has 27 rows and 13 columns as expected. 
The 4 films without scores or box office data remain in the dataset with `NA` values — this is intentional since we used `left_join`, 
which keeps all rows from `pixar_films` regardless of whether a match exists in the other tables.

```{r data_merging}
# Merging datasets using left_join to preserve the main film list
pixar_master <- pixar_films %>%
  left_join(pixar_ratings, by = "film") %>%
  left_join(pixar_box_office, by = "film")

# Verifying the merged structure
str(pixar_master)
nrow(pixar_master)
ncol(pixar_master)

```
### 2.2.Handling Missing Values and Column Refinement

Real-world datasets often contain "data quality problems" such as missing values (NA) or redundant columns.

In this step we prepare the master dataset for analysis. First, we fix two data type issues identified during inspection: the ``number`` column is converted from text to integer using ``as.integer()``, and the value ``"N/A"`` in ``film_rating`` is converted to a real missing value using ``na_if()``. 

We then check for duplicate films using ``count()`` — no duplicates were found, confirming each film appears exactly once. 

Next, we remove the 4 films without data using ``drop_na(rotten_tomatoes)`` since they have no critic scores or box office data, making them unsuitable for analysis. 

Finally, we rename ``film`` to ``movie_title`` for clarity. The missing value audit confirms that only three columns still contain ``NA`` values: ``critics_choice`` (2 missing — *Toy Story* and *A Bug's Life*, released before the Critics' Choice Awards covered animated films), ``cinema_score`` (1 missing) and ``box_office_us_canada`` (1 missing). The last two both belong to *Soul*, which was released directly on Disney+ during the COVID-19 pandemic and therefore has no CinemaScore poll and no North American theatrical gross. These rows are kept intentionally because the variables we model on are complete.


```{r}
# Fix number column from text to integer
# Fix "N/A" in film_rating to real NA
pixar_master <- pixar_master %>%
  mutate(
    number = as.integer(number),
    film_rating = na_if(film_rating, "N/A")
  )

str(pixar_master)
```
```{r}
# Check for duplicate films
pixar_master %>%
  count(film) %>%
  filter(n > 1)

```

```{r data_cleaning}

pixar_clean <- pixar_master %>%
  # Dropping rows with missing rating data
  drop_na(rotten_tomatoes) %>%
  # Renaming the key column for clarity
  rename(movie_title = film)

# Performing a missing-value audit across the final dataset
pixar_clean %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x))))


```
```{r}
# Check unique values in film_rating
pixar_clean %>%
  distinct(film_rating)
```

### 2.3. Reasoning and Data Quality Check
As part of our quality checklist, we summarize the key decisions made during the cleaning process:

ID Uniqueness: We verified using count() that each film appears exactly once in the dataset. No duplicate rows were found.

Missing Observations: We removed the 4 films without data using drop_na(rotten_tomatoes) since they had no critic scores or box office data. The remaining missing values in critics_choice (two early films), cinema_score and box_office_us_canada (both *Soul*) were kept intentionally — removing them would mean losing valuable box office and rating data for well-known films.

Data Type Corrections: number was converted from text to integer and "N/A" in film_rating was replaced with a proper NA using na_if().


This "Master Dataset" contains 23 films and 13 variables and is now ready for the next phase of our analytical report.

```{r}
# Final look at the clean dataset
str(pixar_clean)
head(pixar_clean)
```
## 3. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

### 3.1 Variable Description

We begin by inspecting the structure of the dataset to understand the variable types and dimensions. We then compute basic descriptive statistics for all variables to get an initial sense of the data.

```{r}
str(pixar_clean)
```
```{r}
summary(pixar_clean)
```

### 3.2 New Variables and trends

We create three foundational variables. `release_year` extracts the year from `release_date` using `year()`, giving us a numeric variable we can use for trend analysis. `decade` uses `case_when()` to group films into their respective decades, allowing us to compare Pixar's output across time periods. Finally, `profit` is calculated as the difference between `box_office_worldwide` and `budget`, giving us a direct measure of each film's financial return.

```{r}
pixar_eda <- pixar_clean %>%
  mutate(
    
    #1. release year from date
    release_year = as.integer(year(release_date)),
    
    #2. Decade the film was released in
    decade = case_when(
      release_year < 2000 ~ "1990s",
      release_year < 2010 ~ "2000s",
      release_year < 2020 ~ "2010s",
      TRUE ~ "2020s"
    ),
    
    #3. profit
    profit = box_office_worldwide - budget
  )

pixar_eda %>%
  select(movie_title, release_date, release_year, decade, budget, box_office_worldwide, profit) %>%
  head(10)
```

Next, we create three variables related to financial performance and critical reception. `roi` measures the return on investment as a percentage, calculated by dividing `profit` by budget and multiplying by 100 — for example, Toy Story achieved an ROI of over 1100%, reflecting its enormous commercial success relative to its budget. `avg_critic_score` takes the average of `rotten_tomatoes` and `metacritic` to create a single combined critic score for each film. Finally, `commercial_success` uses `if_else()` to create a simple yes/no flag indicating whether a film made a profit.

```{r}
pixar_eda <- pixar_eda %>%
  mutate(
    # 4. Return on investment as percentage
    roi = ((box_office_worldwide - budget) / budget) * 100,
    
    # 5. Average critic score
    avg_critic_score = (rotten_tomatoes + metacritic) / 2,
    
    # 6. Was the film profitable
    commercial_success = if_else(profit > 0, "Yes", "No")
  )

# Check the new columns
pixar_eda %>%
  select(movie_title, profit, roi, avg_critic_score, commercial_success) %>%
  head(10)
```

In the final group of new variables, we create four categorical columns. `era` uses `case_when()` to divide Pixar's history into three periods — Early Pixar (up to 2005), Golden Age (2006 to 2012), and Modern Pixar (2013 onwards) — reflecting distinct phases in the studio's creative and commercial development. `runtime_category` classifies each film as Short (under 95 minutes), Medium (95 to 110 minutes), or Long (over 110 minutes). `is_sequel` flags sequels and prequels using an explicit list of titles. (A simple pattern match on numbers in the title would miss *Monsters University* and *Finding Dory*.) Finally, `budget_category` groups films into Low, Medium, and High budget tiers based on their production budget.

```{r}
pixar_eda <- pixar_eda %>%
  mutate(
    # 7. era of Pixar filmmaking
    era = case_when(
      release_year <= 2005 ~ "Early Pixar",
      release_year <= 2012 ~ "Golden Age",
      TRUE ~ "Modern Pixar"
    ),
    
    # 8. Runtime category
    runtime_category = case_when(
      run_time < 95 ~ "Short",
      run_time <= 110 ~ "Medium",
      TRUE ~ "Long"
    ),
    
    # 9. sequel or not
    is_sequel = if_else(
      movie_title %in% c("Toy Story 2", "Toy Story 3", "Toy Story 4",
                         "Cars 2", "Cars 3", "Monsters University",
                         "Finding Dory", "Incredibles 2"),
      "Yes", "No"
    ),
    
    # 10. Budget category
    budget_category = case_when(
      budget < 100000000 ~ "Low",
      budget <= 175000000 ~ "Medium",
      TRUE ~ "High"
    )
  )

pixar_eda %>%
  select(movie_title, era, runtime_category, is_sequel, budget_category) %>%
  head(10)
```
  
```{r}

str(pixar_eda)
head(pixar_eda)


pixar_eda %>%
  select(release_year, decade, profit, roi, avg_critic_score, 
         commercial_success, era, runtime_category, is_sequel, budget_category) %>%
  summary()
```
  
In the previous step we notice that `Soul` has a missing value in `box_office_us_canada` while `box_office_worldwide` is available. This film also recorded a negative profit of approximately -$39.6 million. It is one of only two films in the dataset that lost money — the other is *Onward* (-$33 million), whose theatrical run was cut short by the COVID-19 cinema closures.

```{r}
# which film has missing box office data
pixar_eda %>%
  filter(is.na(box_office_us_canada)) %>%
  select(movie_title, budget, box_office_us_canada, box_office_worldwide, profit, roi)
```

```{r}
# Average critic score and profit by era
pixar_eda %>%
  group_by(era) %>%
  summarise(
    number_of_films = n(),
    avg_rt_score = mean(rotten_tomatoes, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_metacritic = mean(metacritic, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_profit = mean(profit, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_roi = mean(roi, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

Early Pixar films had the highest critic scores on both Rotten Tomatoes (97.3) and Metacritic (86.5). The ROI was also highest in this period at about 611%, meaning early films made back much more money relative to their budget. 

Modern Pixar has the most films (10) but the lowest Metacritic score (75) and lowest ROI (256%). 

Interestingly, the average profit is very similar across all three eras — around $470-490 million — suggesting that while Metacritic scores and ROI have declined over time, Pixar films have remained consistently profitable in absolute terms. (Rotten Tomatoes scores do not decline steadily: the Golden Age has the lowest average, 82.7, mainly because of *Cars 2*.)


```{r}
# Profit and ROI by sequel status
pixar_eda %>%
  group_by(is_sequel) %>%
  summarise(
    number_of_films = n(),
    avg_profit = mean(profit, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_roi = mean(roi, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_rt_score = mean(rotten_tomatoes, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

Sequels (8 films) earn more profit on average (about $641 million vs $393 million for the 15 originals), likely because they already have an established audience. However the ROI is almost identical between the two groups (about 354% each), and sequels are reviewed less favourably (average Rotten Tomatoes score 83.9 vs 92.0).

### 3.3 Charts 

Chart 1: Distribution of Rotten Tomatoes Scores
We create this chart to understand how critic scores are distributed across all Pixar films. 

```{r}
ggplot(pixar_eda, aes(x = rotten_tomatoes)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Rotten Tomatoes Scores",
    x = "Rotten Tomatoes Score",
    y = "Number of Films"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
- Most films score between 80 and 100 — the bars are tallest on the right side
- There is one film scoring around 40 — *Cars 2*, the clear low outlier
- The distribution is left skewed — most Pixar films are very well reviewed, with only two scoring below 70 (*Cars 2* and *Cars 3*)

Chart 2: Critic Scores Over Time
We create this chart to see whether Pixar's critical reception has changed over the years.


```{r}
ggplot(pixar_eda, aes(x = release_year, y = rotten_tomatoes)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Rotten Tomatoes Scores Over Time",
    x = "Release Year",
    y = "Rotten Tomatoes Score"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
The scatterplot shows that Pixar's earliest films were consistently highly rated, with almost all scoring above 90. From around 2010 onwards the scores become more variable, with two clear low points: *Cars 2* (2011, 40) and *Cars 3* (2017, 69).


Chart 3: Average Profit by Era
We create this chart to compare the financial performance of Pixar films across the three eras.

```{r}
pixar_eda %>%
  group_by(era) %>%
  summarise(avg_profit = mean(profit, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = era, y = avg_profit / 1000000)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Average Profit by Era",
    x = "Era",
    y = "Average Profit (USD Millions)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The bar chart confirms what we found in the grouped summary — average profit is remarkably consistent across all three eras, ranging between $470 and $490 million. This suggests Pixar has maintained a stable level of commercial success throughout its history.


Chart 4: ROI by Budget Category
We create this chart to explore whether films with lower budgets tend to deliver better returns on investment. 


```{r}
ggplot(pixar_eda, aes(x = budget_category, y = roi)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Return on Investment by Budget Category",
    x = "Budget Category",
    y = "ROI (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The boxplot shows that low budget films achieved the highest median ROI, with a wide spread indicating that some films in this category performed exceptionally well relative to their cost. 

High and medium budget films show lower and more consistent returns, suggesting that bigger budgets do not necessarily lead to better financial efficiency.


Chart 5: Budget vs Worldwide Box Office
We create this chart to explore whether films with higher budgets tend to earn more at the box office. 


```{r}
ggplot(pixar_eda, aes(x = budget / 1000000, y = box_office_worldwide / 1000000)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Budget vs Worldwide Box Office",
    x = "Budget (USD Millions)",
    y = "Worldwide Box Office (USD Millions)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
The scatterplot shows a positive but weak relationship between budget and worldwide box office revenue (correlation of about 0.34) — films with higher budgets tend to earn somewhat more, but there is a lot of spread at every budget level. 

Two $175 million films clearly underperformed at the box office: *Soul* and *Onward*, both released during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Chart 6: Profit Comparison Between Sequels and Original Films
We create this chart to compare the financial performance of sequels versus original films. 


```{r}
ggplot(pixar_eda, aes(x = is_sequel, y = profit / 1000000)) +
```

Original films show a lower median, with the bottom of the distribution formed by *Onward* and *Soul*, which made a small loss.

Overall, the EDA reveals that Pixar films are generally profitable and well reviewed. Early films had the highest critic scores and ROI, sequels earn more than originals, and higher budgets tend to lead to higher box office revenue. These findings will guide our modeling section.



## 4. Modeling

In this section we build two statistical models to answer specific analytical questions about Pixar films.

**Question 1:** Can we predict a Pixar film's worldwide box office revenue based on its budget and critic scores?
We will use **linear regression** to answer this question, as we are predicting a continuous numeric outcome.

**Question 2:** Can we predict whether a Pixar film will be commercially successful based on its budget, critic scores and runtime?
We will use **logistic regression** to answer this question, as the outcome is binary — a film either made a profit (Yes) or did not (No).




### 4.1 Linear Regression: Predicting Worldwide Box Office Revenue

We use linear regression to predict box_office_worldwide based on budget, rotten_tomatoes, and metacritic. 
These predictors were chosen because our EDA showed a positive relationship between budget and box office revenue, 
and critic scores are central to our research question about critical acclaim and financial performance.


```{r}
# Set seed 
set.seed(314)

# Split data into training (75%) and testing (25%)
pixar_split <- initial_split(pixar_eda, prop = 0.75)

pixar_training <- training(pixar_split)
pixar_test <- testing(pixar_split)

cat("Training set:", nrow(pixar_training), "films\n")
cat("Testing set:", nrow(pixar_test), "films\n")

```

Since our dataset is small (23 films), the training set contains 17 films and the testing set contains 6. 

This is a limitation of this dataset when evaluating the model.


```{r}

lm_model_spec <- linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm") %>%
  set_mode("regression")


lm_fit <- lm_model_spec %>%
  fit(box_office_worldwide ~ budget + rotten_tomatoes + metacritic, 
      data = pixar_training)

summary(lm_fit$fit)

```
The `budget` coefficient has a p-value of 0.0025, which is well below 0.05, 
meaning it is statistically significant in the training data. 
The estimate of 4.38 means that, holding critic scores constant, each extra dollar of budget 
is associated with approximately $4.38 more at the box office. This is an association, not a causal effect — 
bigger budgets also tend to go to franchise films with a built-in audience.


The `metacritic` coefficient has a p-value of 0.0255, 
which is just below 0.05, meaning it is also statistically significant. 
The estimate of 18,170,000 means that each additional point on the
Metacritic scale is associated with around $18 million more in worldwide revenue.

The `rotten_tomatoes` coefficient has a p-value of 0.82, which is far above 0.05, 
meaning it is not statistically significant. 
We cannot conclude that Rotten Tomatoes score has a meaningful effect on box office revenue 
when budget and Metacritic are already included in the model. Part of the reason is that the two critic scores 
are strongly correlated (r ≈ 0.80), so they largely carry the same information (multicollinearity).

The R-squared value of 0.58 means the model explains 58% of the variation in worldwide box office revenue. 
The overall model p-value of 0.008 confirms the model as a whole is statistically significant.


```{r}

# Predictions
lm_predictions <- lm_fit %>%
  predict(new_data = pixar_test) %>%
  bind_cols(pixar_test %>% select(movie_title, box_office_worldwide))

# View predictions vs actual values
lm_predictions


```

```{r}
# Performance metrics
metrics(lm_predictions, 
        truth = box_office_worldwide, 
        estimate = .pred)
```

When we evaluate the model on the 6 test films, the results are weaker than on the training data. 
The R-squared drops from 0.58 on the training set to just 0.065 on the test set, 
meaning the model explains very little of the variation in box office revenue for unseen films. 

The RMSE is about $356 million and the MAE (the average absolute error) is about $260 million — a very large error relative to a median box office of about $624 million. 
The RMSE is higher than the MAE because it penalizes large errors more heavily, such as the prediction for Soul. 
The large gap between training and test performance is likely due to two reasons 
— the very small dataset of only 23 films makes it difficult to build a reliable model, 
and Soul is an extreme outlier in the test set, having earned far less than expected due to its unusual release circumstances.

These results highlight the limitations of modeling with such a small dataset.



### 4.2 Logistic Regression: Predicting Commercial Success

We use logistic regression to predict whether a Pixar film will be commercially successful — meaning it made a profit. 
The outcome variable is `commercial_success` (Yes or No), which we created during the EDA stage. 

We use `budget`, `rotten_tomatoes`, `metacritic`, and `run_time` as predictors. 
Logistic regression is appropriate here because the outcome is binary rather than numeric.


```{r}
# Prepare the data
pixar_log <- pixar_eda %>%
  mutate(commercial_success = as.factor(commercial_success))

# Check factor levels
levels(pixar_log$commercial_success)

```
```{r}
# Reorder so "Yes" is the first level (positive class)
pixar_log <- pixar_log %>%
  mutate(commercial_success = factor(commercial_success, levels = c("Yes", "No")))

# Confirm the order
levels(pixar_log$commercial_success)
```

```{r}
# Split the data
set.seed(314)

log_split <- initial_split(pixar_log, prop = 0.75, strata = commercial_success)

log_training <- training(log_split)
log_test <- testing(log_split)

cat("Training set:", nrow(log_training), "films\n")
cat("Testing set:", nrow(log_test), "films\n")

```
```{r}
# Define logistic regression model specification
log_model_spec <- logistic_reg() %>%
  set_engine("glm") %>%
  set_mode("classification")

# Train the model
log_fit <- log_model_spec %>%
  fit(commercial_success ~ budget + rotten_tomatoes + metacritic + run_time,
      data = log_training)

# View
summary(log_fit$fit)
```
The logistic regression results show that none of the predictors — 
`budget`, `rotten_tomatoes`, `metacritic`, or `run_time` — are statistically significant, as all p-values are well above 0.05. 

This means we cannot reliably predict commercial success from these variables. 
However this result is not surprising given the nature of the data — 
almost all Pixar films in our dataset made a profit, with only two exceptions (*Onward* and *Soul*). 
Because the split is stratified, one of them (*Soul*) ended up in the training set and the other (*Onward*) in the test set, 
so the model was trained on just a single unsuccessful film. 
When nearly all outcomes are the same (Yes), the model has very little variation to learn from, 
making it very difficult to identify meaningful predictors.

```{r}
# Predictions

log_predictions <- log_fit %>%
  predict(new_data = log_test) %>%
  bind_cols(log_fit %>% 
              predict(new_data = log_test, type = "prob")) %>%
  bind_cols(log_test %>% select(movie_title, commercial_success))

# View 
log_predictions

```

```{r}

# performance metrics
accuracy(log_predictions, 
         truth = commercial_success, 
         estimate = .pred_class)

```
The model correctly predicted 5 out of 6 films, achieving an accuracy of 83.3%. 
However this result should be interpreted carefully. 
The model predicted "Yes" for every single film, 
which means it did not actually learn to distinguish between successful and unsuccessful films — 
it simply defaulted to the majority class. Onward was the only film predicted incorrectly. 

This confirms what we saw in the coefficients — with almost all films being commercially successful, 
the model has very little to learn from and the high accuracy is misleading rather than meaningful.


### 4.3 Model Comparison

We built two models to answer our analytical questions. Here we compare them across several dimensions.

Predicting ability: The linear regression model showed a reasonable fit on the training data (R-squared = 0.58) 
but performed poorly on the test set (R-squared = 0.065), with an RMSE of $356 million and an MAE of $260 million. 
The logistic regression model achieved 83.3% accuracy but only by predicting "Yes" for every film, which is not genuinely useful.

Statistical significance: In the linear regression model, budget and metacritic were statistically significant predictors. 
In the logistic regression model, none of the predictors were statistically significant.

Limitations: Both models are heavily limited by the small dataset of only 23 films. 
With so few observations, it is difficult to build reliable models that generalize well to new data. 
The logistic regression was further limited by class imbalance — almost all films were commercially successful, 
leaving very little variation for the model to learn from.

Conclusion: Between the two models, linear regression performed better in terms of meaningful results. 
It identified budget and Metacritic score as significant predictors of box office revenue in the training data, 
which is broadly consistent with our EDA findings, although the weak test-set performance means these results should not be over-interpreted. 
The logistic regression was not able to produce useful predictions given the nature of the data.



## 5. Summary and Reflection

### 5.1 Project Summary and Main Findings
In this project, we analyzed the Pixar Film Ratings dataset to explore the relationship between critical acclaim, budget, and commercial success. We successfully integrated three distinct tables into a clean Master Dataset, engineered 10 new variables (such as `profit`, `roi`, `era`, and `is_sequel`), and visualized key industry trends. 

Our main findings indicate that while early Pixar films achieved the highest critical scores and Return on Investment (ROI), the studio has maintained remarkably consistent absolute profit margins across all its eras. Furthermore, our linear regression model found that production budget and Metacritic scores were statistically significant predictors of a film's worldwide box office revenue on the training data — although the model generalized poorly to the test films, so this finding is tentative.

### 5.2 Difficulties and Limitations
The most difficult part of the project was building reliable predictive models. Our dataset was extremely small (only 23 films after cleaning), which severely limited our models' ability to generalize. This was evident in our linear regression model, which fit the training data well but performed poorly on the test set. 

Additionally, modeling commercial success using logistic regression was highly challenging due to extreme class imbalance. Because almost every Pixar film in history has been profitable, the model had almost no "unsuccessful" examples to learn from, resulting in a misleadingly high accuracy where the model simply predicted "Yes" for everything. Finally, dealing with outliers — specifically *Soul* and *Onward*, the only two unprofitable films, both affected by the COVID-19 pandemic — significantly skewed our test predictions.

### 5.3 Reflection and Future Improvements
The most interesting part of the analytical process was discovering the financial dynamics of sequels versus original films. It was fascinating to see that while sequels reliably generate higher absolute profits due to established fanbases, their actual financial efficiency (ROI) is almost identical to riskier original films.

If we were to start this project again, or if we had more time and resources, we would not limit ourselves to just Pixar. We would expand our dataset to include all Walt Disney Animation Studios and DreamWorks Animation films. This would dramatically increase our sample size, introduce a balanced mix of profitable and unprofitable films for our logistic regression, and allow us to build much more robust and trustworthy machine learning models.
